# Scripts and programs {#sec-scripts-and-programs}

Every number and figure in this book comes from a script under `scripts/`,
run against real code, not pasted in by hand. This chapter is the index: what
each script does, what it needs, and how to run it. It groups scripts by what
they are for rather than by chapter, because several scripts serve more than
one chapter and a few (the benchmarks, the course runners) serve none
directly.

Three conventions hold across all of them unless a script says otherwise:

* output goes under `.build/review/<name>` or `.build/<name>` as JSON,
  `.npz` arrays and PNG figures, never into the source tree;
* `--input` for a script that reads a stored shower takes the path to a
  private G4 HDF5 file (`sim_e_100GeV_10.h5`-style); no such file is shipped
  in the repository, and scripts that need one are unusable without it;
* every script is run from the repository root with `src/` on
  `PYTHONPATH`, e.g. `PYTHONPATH=src python scripts/<name>.py --help`.

## Production runs {#sec-scripts-production}

These are the scripts that answer "how does the whole thing perform on a
real event, over the real array" — the ones a result in the book traces back
to.

**`run_shower_moments.py`** — the moment route against an element-by-element
reference, on one real stored shower. Reports how many angular channels the
summed response needs before it stops moving, the moment route's error and
cost against the direct sum at matched settings (block count and polynomial
degree scanned), and the closed-form ballistic term's own cost, so the floor
of the total time is visible next to the part that is actually expanded.
Since this turn, both the radial-moment lookup (`KernelChannels` →
`ResponseCache.moments_at`) and the ballistic term go through the fast paths
by default — `PreparedMultipoles` (`spline_fast.py`) and
`vectorised_ballistic_fast` (`ballistic_fast.py`) — falling back to the
plain scipy/numpy implementations only when numba is unavailable; the report
records which backend actually ran under `cache.spline_backend` and
`ballistic.backend`.

```
python scripts/run_shower_moments.py --input /path/sim_e_100GeV_10.h5 \
    --event 5 --output .build/review/shower-moments
```

**`run_shower_axial.py`** — the production run of the sparse axial
("needle") representation of @sec-axial-source: one G4 event, the full
array, the full frequency window, charges and time bins, end to end and
timed. Since this turn it also goes through the fast paths by default,
same as `run_shower_moments.py`: `PreparedMultipoles` for every
`KernelChannels` lookup (the main run and the refinement scan alike) and
`vectorised_ballistic_fast` for the ballistic term, with the backend that
actually ran recorded under `cache.spline_backend` and `ballistic.backend`.

**`run_shower_axial_bins.py`** — time bins of a stored shower on a window
chosen to actually contain the light, rather than the default frequency
grid's reconstructible range; needed because the spectrum of a module tens
of metres away carries arrival times well past what a coarse frequency
spacing can invert cleanly. Also wrapped with `PreparedMultipoles` by
default since this turn; the report's `cache_spline_backend` says which
backend ran.

**`run_shower_frequency.py`** — the moment route at nonzero frequency, where
the criterion for how large a block may be changes from a purely geometric
one (`extent / distance`) to one that also has to track how fast the kernel
oscillates in `omega`.

**`run_segment_event.py`** — a small, hand-built multi-segment event (eight
straight Cherenkov segments: a kinked primary plus five delayed branches),
computed in three rigid poses (original, translated, rotated) from one
cache, with the invariance checks of @sec-cone-segment (joint
rotation+translation, time shift, yield linearity, segment splitting) run
against it every time. Since this turn the single-band cache is wrapped with
`PreparedMultipoles` before any `segment_spectrum` call; the report's
`cache.spline_backend` says whether that wrapping actually happened.

```
python scripts/run_segment_event.py --output .build/review/event
```

**`run_effective_segments.py`** — method 7
(`lighthit.experimental.effective_segments`, not yet its own book chapter)
on a real stored shower: test the hypothesis that it can be reduced to a
chosen number `K` of straight segments and report,
for every `K` in `--segments`, how many pieces were built, how far orders 1
and `>=2` are from the same element-by-element reference
`run_shower_moments.py` uses (monotonic shrinkage is a result to test, not a
property of the construction), that the ballistic order is bit-for-bit
independent of `K` (it is
never taken from the segment fit — always the closed form), and the
wall-clock cost of fitting and applying the method at every `K`, at both a
handful of control receivers and the full array.

```
python scripts/run_effective_segments.py --input /path/sim_e_100GeV_10.h5 \
    --event 5 --segments 1 2 4 8 16 32 64 \
    --output .build/review/effective-segments
```

**`run_method_survey.py`** — every method that produces light transport, on
one real event and the full array, side by side: ballistic (shared,
computed once), the moment route (`evaluate_moments`), the conservative 3-D
and pure 1-D axial routes (using `axial_fast` when available), and method 7
(`full_response`). `direct_response` — the
slowest, most honest method — is deliberately excluded from the routine
comparison and used only at a handful of control modules to score the
other compact routes, never run over the full array. Each method's report block
carries its per-order error against that reference, its apply time over
the full array, and the scattered (order `>=1`) charge total, so the compact
routes and the shared ballistic term can be read off one file instead of
three separate script runs.

```
python scripts/run_method_survey.py --input /path/sim_e_100GeV_10.h5 \
    --event 5 --output .build/review/method-survey
```

**`run_baikal_clusters.py`** — a laser flash as seen by three Baikal-GVD-like
clusters, through the cache, using published Baikal-GVD geometry and laser
parameters against the repository's synthetic water.  Its sampled uncached
control solve explicitly uses the Numba angular backend.

**`build_cache.py`** — builds the three-band cache actually shipped for the
Baikal-like geometry (`10–20 m`, `20–60 m`, `60–400 m`, with band-specific
`k_max`/degree/radii), saves it to `docs/cache-baikal/cache.npz`, and runs
the off-grid interpolation and finite-`L` consistency checks against it. Not
parametrised by `argparse`; edit `BANDS` in the script to change the bands.
The production build explicitly selects the Numba angular backend and thus
requires the `accelerate` extra.

**`run_event_viewer.py`** — the local production viewer run. It reads every
HDF5 file under `g4_data` (or explicit `--input` paths), evaluates event 5 by
default with `compile_axial_source_fast` and `PreparedAxialKernel.apply`, adds
the exact per-element ballistic arrivals, and appends an isotropic point-laser
event. One shared Numba transport cache serves every event. Outputs stay under
`.build/event-viewer`: per-event NPZ files, portable `viewer.json`, and one
self-contained `viewer.html` with module charges, time histograms, a full-array
heatmap and time animation.

Before a full spectrum is applied, a 64-cell absorption-only axial proxy and
exact ballistic charge make an initial threshold mask. Rejected OMs receive an
exact axial $\omega=0$ guard; only those still below the configured photoelectron
threshold omit their nonzero-frequency calculation. The local audit and
speedups are in `research/signal-screening.md`.

## Benchmarks {#sec-scripts-benchmarks}

Benchmarks measure cost, not correctness; they are not part of the
validation suite and can be skipped in a plain read-through of the physics.

**`benchmark_backends.py`** — numpy against numba for both the angular tail
and the exact-first-order scalar kernel on the same complete public
point-Green problem, after `pip install .[accelerate]`.

**`benchmark_route.py`** — the cost of the whole route: build, save, load,
apply, reuse, read out.

**`benchmark_moment_route.py`** — the moment route against the element sum
*at matched accuracy*, because an error table alone says which settings are
accurate but not whether the route is actually worth using at that accuracy.

**`benchmark_axial_fast.py`** — compares the exact-representation
accelerators (the axial/needle fast paths) against local G4 data; nothing
here is published, it is a local-only speed comparison. Supports
`--compare-compilers` to contrast numba source-compile time against numpy.

**`study_time_ringing.py`** — compares finite-frequency inversion of the exact
full-HG first-order spectrum with independent physical-time bins while varying
node count, cutoff and bin width separately. It demonstrates why more nodes at
fixed cutoff do not cure a band-limited front, and why wider bins suppress
visible ringing without recovering omitted high frequencies. Results and
interpretation are in `research/time-ringing.md`.

## Verification and independent controls {#sec-scripts-verification}

Each of these is an independent check of one physical claim, deliberately
built without reusing the machinery it is checking.

**`verify_absorption.py`** — open, independent collimation checks; no
private optics, nothing that could not be published as-is.

**`verify_directionality.py`** — independent controls for the
arrival-direction claims.

**`verify_segment.py`** — independent controls for the finite Cherenkov
segment of @sec-cone-segment.

**`check_shell_resolution.py`** — refines shell width, flight quadrature and
maximum path in the Monte-Carlo cross-check, being careful that changing the
maximum path also changes random-number consumption between photons, which
by itself can look like a cutoff bias if not controlled for.

**`probe_shower_axis.py`** — is a stored shower actually one-dimensional,
and in which of its variables? Builds the photon-weighted principal axis and
reports the event in that frame; this is the script behind the numbers in
@sec-axial-shape.

**`probe_block_channels.py`** — why a higher polynomial block degree stops
helping: the block still has to resolve the spherical harmonics of the
kernel channel, and that is a separate limit from the polynomial one.

## Course and notebooks {#sec-scripts-course}

**`run_course.py`** — executes the course notebooks as separate kernels,
using this script's own Python, writing outputs and machine-readable
evidence to `.build/course`; needs `nbformat`, `nbclient`, `nbconvert` and
`jupyter_client`. Source notebooks are left untouched.

**`run_course_plain.py`** — the same course, one fresh interpreter per
notebook, without Jupyter; the fallback when the `nbclient`/`nbconvert`
stack is not available.

**`strip_notebook_outputs.py`** — removes notebook outputs and execution
counts before a public git commit, so a diff shows the source change and
not a wall of regenerated cell output.

## Utilities {#sec-scripts-utilities}

**`compare_runs.py`** — compares two CLI runs on identical observations,
bins and source normalisation; useful for checking that a code change left
a result numerically where it was.

## Tests, as distinct from scripts {#sec-scripts-tests}

`tests/` is not covered above because it is not run by hand for a result —
it is the correctness suite, run with `pytest` (or, in an environment
without real `pytest`/`numba`, the local shim under
`scratch/shim/run_tests.py`, which is not part of the repository and exists
only to verify correctness without those packages installed). Test files
worth knowing about because they anchor the fast paths this chapter
describes: `test_ballistic_fast.py`, `test_spline_fast.py`,
`test_cache_build_vectorised.py` and `test_effective_segments.py` each
check a fast path against the plain implementation it replaces or wraps,
never against itself.
